1.point: The Munajat's confession of a wasted life is the kind of repentance that opens the road; this chapter sets out the first stage (polishing): anyone can begin by repenting, repentance is kept at a steady pace, and the law is kept strictly starting with people.
steps: Contrast habitual istighfar with the Munajat's confession of a whole life spent forgetting God (hook).
Place that confession at the start of the road: of Chapter Eight's four stages the first is polishing, and repentance opens it.
State the chapter's three claims in the words of the section headings.

2.point: The road starts with repentance, and because this repentance covers every sin and every careless attitude towards God, any believer, however bad their past, can begin.
steps: Setting out means waking from heedlessness and then repenting; repentance is the first step of the road.
This repentance reaches beyond sins to casualness towards God.
Because it covers every sin and every wrong attitude, it is open to the sinner as much as the devout; early mystics began as wrongdoers.
What actually holds a sinner back is despair, and the Qur'an (al-Zumar) answers that despair: God forgives all sins.
Repentance is what polishes the heart, which is why it opens the stage called polishing.
Therefore anyone can begin, and the Munajat supplies the words.

3.point: Repentance is renewed every time the traveller falls, taken no faster than the self can bear, and not deferred to old age.
steps: Old habits return; when they do the traveller repents again, so repentance is continuous.
Continuous does not mean casual: the resolve is never to return, and a fall is met with fresh repentance rather than despair.
Habits return because the self strikes back, and when it strikes hard it can floor a traveller.
Because the self strikes back, rushing ahead is dangerous; progress must be gradual (the Tehran story; the Imams' counsel of pace).
Not rushing is not putting off: age makes the road harder but not impossible, so the sooner begun the easier.
Hence: steady, renewed, not rushed, not deferred.

4.point: Beyond repentance, polishing is strict keeping of the shari'a, and the law's first demand on the traveller is to put right their dealings with people.
steps: Polishing means keeping what the Prophet ordered in the strictest sense; without it the traveller cannot move on.
Within the law, the first condition after repentance is good conduct with people; without it no practice carries the traveller forward.
The reason is a system of justice: any wrong done to anyone, even unknowingly, holds the traveller back until it is put right.
What this conduct looks like: the Prophet and Imams were friendly with all, and the pious answer wrongs with kindness.
It reaches down to the smallest courtesy to an ordinary person (Hatim al-Asamm).
Conclusion: polishing begins with repentance, continues as the law, and the law's first demand is people.

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Supplies the hook: reads the displayed Munajat lines as repentance for a whole life of forgetting God, not for a particular wrong. Nothing earlier has done this.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Places that repentance at the opening of the first stage (recalling Chapter Eight in one sentence) and states the chapter's three claims. This is the section's point.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies the first step: setting out is waking then repenting, and repentance is the first step of the road. The Khomeini line confirms the order inside the same paragraph rather than adding a separate link.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: Supplies the second step: this repentance reaches beyond sins to casualness towards God. ¶6 depends on it ('covers every sin and every wrong attitude').

¶5.label: aside
¶5.why: Lantern of the Path says what ¶4 has already said (repentance of the elite is for occupation with other than God) and the elite/common distinction is not used by any later step. Cutting it leaves ¶6 intact; a second source saying the same thing.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Supplies the third step: because repentance covers every sin and attitude it is open to sinners as much as the devout, with Bishr and Fudayl as proof and a lead into the Fudayl box.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Supplies the obstacle that remains once repentance is open to all: despair that the road belongs to people of higher calibre. Sets up the al-Zumar verse.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Answers the obstacle raised in ¶7: the verse's 'excesses against their souls' covers the despairing as well as sinners, and God forgives all sins. The step ¶7 opened closes here.

¶9.label: aside
¶9.why: That sincere repentance also brings God's love and covering is a further fruit of repentance; the point (the road begins with repentance and anyone can begin) does not need it, and no later sentence uses it.

¶10.label: support
¶10.why: Gives the evidence that repentance polishes the heart, which is why the stage is called polishing. ¶2 and ¶3 assert that repentance opens the first stage and ¶24 builds on it ('repentance opens the first stage'); this paragraph is what makes that link visible.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Draws the conclusion for the first time as a conclusion ('anyone can therefore begin') and introduces the Munajat words that make it practical. Marginal: ¶6 already said it is open to sinner and devout alike.

¶12.label: restate
¶12.why: Glosses the quotation and ends by saying again what ¶11 and ¶6 have said: any believer can say these words whatever their past. No new link.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Supplies the first step: when a habit returns the traveller repents again, so repentance is a continuous process.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Refines ¶13 against a possible misreading: steadiness means resolving never to return, and a fall is met with fresh repentance not despair. Tabatabai is used as a counter-view to be reconciled, not as a second voice saying the same thing.

¶15.label: advance
¶15.why: Supplies the cause of the falls: the self fights back at every stage and can leave a traveller reeling. ¶16 depends on it ('because the self can strike back').

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Supplies the step that rushing is dangerous because the self strikes back, names the Imams' counsel of pace (supplied in ¶19), and introduces the story.

¶17.label: support
¶17.why: The Tehran story, first half: the example ¶16 announces and ¶18 draws the lesson from.

¶18.label: support
¶18.why: Completes the story and draws its lesson ('you are rushing'; progress must be built gradually), with the three-month fast as a second illustration. Used by the step in ¶16.

¶19.label: support
¶19.why: Supplies the Imams' counsel of pace that ¶16 referred to ('the pace the Imams advised') and that ¶20 explicitly draws on. Without it ¶16's reference hangs.

¶20.label: aside
¶20.why: Tabatabai's rule of moderation restates the lesson of ¶16-¶19 (do not take on too much at the start) from a further authority. Burnout is a second consequence of rushing that no later step uses; the section's conclusion in ¶23 does not rely on it.

¶21.label: advance
¶21.why: Supplies the other side of the point: not rushing is not putting off; age makes the road harder, not impossible, and deferral is itself despair of God's mercy.

¶22.label: aside
¶22.why: Imam Khomeini saying the same as ¶21 ('the sooner begun the easier'), as the paragraph itself admits: 'the lectures and Imam Khomeini agree'. Second scholar; cutting it loses nothing ¶23 uses.

¶23.label: restate
¶23.why: Summarises ¶13, ¶16 and ¶21 in one sentence. The point has already been reached; this says it again.

¶24.label: advance
¶24.why: Supplies the first step: polishing is keeping the law in the strictest sense, and without it the traveller cannot move on. One-sentence recall of Chapter Six stays within bounds.

¶25.label: advance
¶25.why: Supplies the second step: within the law, the first condition after repentance is conduct towards people; without it no practice carries the traveller forward.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Supplies the reason for ¶25: a system of justice that will not let the traveller rise until wrongs, even unknowing ones, are put right.

¶27.label: aside
¶27.why: Opens by restating what ¶25-¶26 established ('the inner road cannot go around people'), then adds Tabatabai and Amuli saying it again. Two more authorities for a step already made and reasoned; no later sentence uses either quotation.

¶28.label: support
¶28.why: Shows what the condition looks like in practice at the highest station (Prophet and Imams friendly with all) and introduces the oration of Imam Ali, which ¶29 reads. Marginal: 'however high mystics rise' pushes towards a persistence claim the point does not require.

¶29.label: support
¶29.why: Reads the displayed quotation: each clause answers a wrong with a kindness, so the pious are measured by how they treat those who wronged them. Ties the example to 'putting things right with people'. Marginal; stands or falls with ¶28 and the quotation.

¶30.label: support
¶30.why: Extends the condition to the smallest courtesy and sets up the Hatim box, which ¶31 draws on ('down to sparing an ordinary person's embarrassment').

¶31.label: restate
¶31.why: Summarises the whole chapter (sections 2, 3 and 4). Every claim in it has been made already.

¶32.label: aside
¶32.why: First sentence repeats ¶31; the second raises a question the chapter does not answer. Neither adds a link to this section's point.
